notes.text: Testimonium Flavianum: most scholars judge it partly reworked by Christian scribes (e.g. "He was [the] Christ"), while an authentic core about Jesus and Pilate is widely accepted. Not Josephus's own confession.

Onkelos replaces "a hanged man is cursed by God" with "because he sinned before the LORD he was crucified" (אִצְטְלַב, root צלב). Rabbinic halakha, not anti-Christian polemic; Paul says Christ became a curse "for us".

The Aramaic turns "sons of God" into "sons of the great ones" (בְּנֵי רַבְרְבַיָּא), and Metsudah's English of the Hebrew reads "sons of the rulers": both drop the angels. The NT speaks of angels who sinned.
Where the Hebrew has Jacob see God (Elohim) face to face, Onkelos reads "angels of the LORD" (מַלְאָכַיָּא דַּיְיָ): a theological softening, not a different Hebrew text.
Follows the MT "according to the number of the sons of Israel" (בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל), not the "sons of God" (4QDeutj; LXX "angels of God") that Heiser judges original. It witnesses only the MT reading.

The Hebrew "for my name is in him" becomes "for in My Name is his word" (בִשְׁמִי מֵימְרֵהּ, Memra); Metsudah brackets "[his word]". Heiser and Segal cite b. Sanh. 38b for this verse's use in two-powers debates.

Philo calls the Word God's "first-born", "the eldest of his angels" and "archangel". Shared vocabulary, different doctrine: Hebrews sets the Son above the angels, and the Word who is God became flesh.
Philo's Word is "neither being uncreate as God, nor yet created as you" but between the two. John allows no middle category: the Word is God, and all things were made through him.
Philo says the article-less "God" of the Bethel text (Gen 31:13 LXX) means God's "most ancient word", called God only loosely. Not a precedent for "a god" in John 1:1c: the NT calls the Son God.
The "son" the high priest needs "as a paraclete… to procure forgiveness of sins" is, in context (2.133–135), the cosmos whose image he wears, not the Logos or a messiah.
Philo's LXX reads "angels of God" (Gen 6:2), but he holds angels, demons and souls "one and identical" and makes the "angels" wicked men pursuing pleasures. The NT speaks of angels who sinned.

"This is the Son of Man" is Charles's conjectural emendation, universally rejected by scholars (Nickelsburg–VanderKam). The Ethiopic reads "You are that Son of Man", naming Enoch; the NT gives the title to Jesus.
"To him ascribe all sin" makes Azazel the source of all sin. Scripture traces sin's entry to Adam and its root to human desire; 1 Enoch's own 98:4 says "man of himself has created it".
The angel Penemue teaches writing, and death takes hold of men "through this their knowledge". Scripture says death entered through Adam's sin, and God himself commands writing.

Evil spirits as the spirits of the giants: a Second Temple explanation of demons, adopted by Heiser. Scripture names the Nephilim but is silent on where demons come from: compatible with, not taught by, Scripture.
Blesses those who "sin not as the sinners" in reckoning a 364-day year, and faults those who miscount. The NT does not let believers be judged by their calendar.

"My son Jesus… my son Christ" is a Latin Christian scribal change; the Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic and Armenian read "Messiah". This Messiah dies with all flesh after 400 years; Christ, raised, dies no more.
Gap: this KJV/Latin text lacks 4 Ezra 7:36–105 (the "missing fragment", published by Bensly, 1875): souls after death (7:75–101) and the ruling against intercession at the judgment (7:102–105).
"Jesus" here is the KJV's Greek form of Joshua, who prayed for Israel after Achan's sin; not Jesus of Nazareth. The Clementine Latin has no name here.
"The just, which have many good works laid up with thee, shall out of their own deeds receive reward." Paul: a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
The KJV/Latin "waxed strong with the thousands of heaven" differs from the Syriac, Ethiopic, Arabic and Armenian "flew with the clouds of heaven", which echoes Dan 7:13.
The KJV/Latin "two hundred and four" books is 94 in other versions: 24 made public (the Hebrew Bible's count) and 70 kept secret as the "fountain of wisdom". Scripture presents itself as sufficient.
Line 18: "the Watchers of heaven fell" rests on an editor's correction: the medieval Genizah manuscript reads עידי ("witnesses"), corrected to עירי ("Watchers"). Retells the Enochic Watchers story.
Lines 3–4 name "the book of the divisions of the times into their jubilees and their weeks" (Jubilees) as the exact authority on Israel's times. Jubilees, with its 364-day calendar, is not Scripture.

Line 19: "[until the arising of the messia]h of Aaron and Israel" is mostly restored; "and he will atone for their iniquity" survives, but its subject (God or the Messiah) is unstated. Not proof of an atoning messiah.

Lines 15–17 are largely restored: "lame or deaf" and "for the holy angels are in your midst" are wholly in editorial brackets (compare 1QSa 2:8–9, where the angel clause survives). Do not cite them as CD's text.
Line 11: the first ordinances bind "until the coming of a prophet and the messiahs of Aaron and Israel" (plural). Hebrews has one priest-king from Judah, "not after the order of Aaron".

The divine name is written as the cipher הואהא (line 13) and, in the Isa 40:3 quotation, as four dots shown as יייי (line 14); neither is a word to translate. The scroll applies Isa 40:3 to Torah study.

Lines 11–12, "when [God] begets the Messiah": "God" (אל) is wholly restored, the verb has a damaged letter, and its reading is disputed (יוליד "begets" or יוליך "leads forth"). Do not use as evidence.
Line 17, the Hab 2:4b lemma "the righteous shall live by his faith", is wholly an editor's restoration. The scroll is no evidence for the MT "by his faith" over the LXX "by my faith".

Lines 1–3 apply Hab 2:4b to "the doers of the Torah in the house of Judah", saved for "their toil and their faith" (or fidelity) "in the Teacher of Righteousness". Paul uses it to set faith apart from works of the law.

Lines 9–11: members are "to love all the sons of light… and to hate all the sons of darkness". Fairly, 10:17–20 renounces repaying evil and leaves judgment to God (cf. Rom 12:19), awaiting "the day of vengeance".

Lines 13–14: an animal that falls into a cistern or pit is not to be lifted out on the Sabbath; 16–17: a person fallen into water is not to be brought up with a ladder, rope or utensil. Jesus treats rescue as right.

Lines 3–9 bar from the assembly anyone lame, blind, deaf, dumb, crippled in hands or feet, or blemished, "for holy angels" are in their [congregation] (line 9 partly restored). Jesus invites the crippled, lame and blind.

Line 19: "those who entered the new covenant in the land of Damascus" (cf. 19:33–34; 20:12), the sect's claim to Jeremiah's new covenant. Jesus speaks of "the new covenant in my blood"; Hebrews applies Jer 31 to Christ.
Line 12: "the covenant and pact they established in the land of Damascus, that is the new covenant", the sect's claim to Jeremiah's new covenant. Jesus speaks of "the new covenant in my blood".
Death and Yom Kippur atone "together with repentance"; for graver sins repentance suspends punishment until Yom Kippur. Hebrews: animal blood cannot take away sins, and Christ was offered once.
The condemned man confesses, or says "may my death be an expiation for all my sins". Hebrews grounds atonement in Christ's single offering to bear the sins of many.
Kulp's reference "(Josh. 7:35)" is an error: the Hebrew cites Josh 7:25 (Joshua 7 has 26 verses).
Grounds a share in the world to come in belonging to Israel, minus listed exclusions. Like Jesus, it holds that the Torah teaches resurrection; but the NT grounds the share in Christ, not descent.
Kulp's "non-canonical books" renders ספרים החיצונים, "external books"; which books Akiva meant is debated. Not a ruling on the Protestant Apocrypha. "A biblical doctrine" renders "from the Torah".

"Greater stringency" for the scribes' teachings than for the Torah: an elder who adds to scribal rulings is liable, one who denies a Torah command exempt. Jesus faults setting aside God's command for tradition.
A chain of transmission from Sinai through the elders, ending "make a fence round the Torah". The Hebrew says "Torah", not "Oral Torah". Jesus rejects the elders' tradition where it voids God's word.

Applies Ps 82:1 to the Shekhinah present with groups of Jews: ten for "the congregation of God", three for "in the midst of the judges" (Hebrew elohim). A homily; Heiser reads these elohim as God's divine council.
The Passover meal as codified c. AD 200. Bokser argues it reads post-70 practice back into Temple times: use it as a later parallel to the Last Supper (Mark 14:12–26), not as its order of service.
Kulp's reference "(Deuteronomy 6:20-25)" is an error: "A wandering Aramean was my father" is Deut 26:5.
